newsitem.title: PERU: Peru quake traps 300 miners; seven people killed.
newsitem.headline: Peru quake traps 300 miners; seven people killed.

text.p: A powerful earthquake pounded southern Peru on Tuesday, trapping about 300 gold miners underground and leaving hundreds injured and at least seven dead, officials said.
Officials said more than 500 people may have been injured in the quake, which was felt throughout central Peru and shook the capital Lima for a minute.

The hardest hit towns appeared to be Nazca, about 290 miles (460 km) south of Lima, and Ica, a nearby town on the Pacific Coast. Army officials said about 300 people were hurt in Nazca and 200 were injured in Ica. Most of the injuries occurred when buildings collapsed.
"It was intense. We had to fly -- all of us. The roof of our house practically fell on top of us. There's so much damage," said Nazca resident Adrian Contreras.
Landslides at the Huanca gold mine, 310 miles (500 km) south of Lima on the border of the departments of Ica and Ayacucho, trapped 300 miners, Jorge Rodriguez, a police doctor in Ayacucho, said.
"What's tragic is that all road access (from Ayacucho) has been cut off. We need urgent help by air," Rodriguez said, adding that some rescue workers had arrived from Ica.
The underground mine is one of many that have developed haphazardly in Peru's gold sector, where miners usually do not work for registered companies and use primitive technology.
The quake caused the collapse of several other small mines in the two departments, seriously injuring at least four people, local mining unions and rescue workers said.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake measured 7.3 on the Richter scale and its epicentre was 65 miles (100 km) southeast of Ica.
"It is a major earthquake," said John Minch, a geophysicist at the National Earthquake Information Centre in Golden, Colorado. He said the quake occurred at noon Peru time (1700 GMT).
Five of the deaths occurred in Nazca, where 40 percent of the houses suffered serious damage.

Two children and one teenager died from head wounds caused by falling debris, and two men were killed when a landslide demolished homes in one of Nazca's many shantytowns, according to army Gen. Rolando Quezada, who was coordinating rescue work.
A man in neighbouring Ica died of a heart attack brought on by the earthquake, Col. Lucio Corpuera, a Civil Defence official in Lima, said.
In Acari, near Peru's second city, Arequipa, 640 miles (1,030 km) south of Lima, a 60-year old woman died in the quake, Corpuera added without giving more details.
In Nazca, medical workers attended to 120 injured people, 40 of whom were in serious condition, Fermin Caceres, director of the Nazca hospital, said.
"The majority are women, children and the elderly, who could not run away from the falling walls," Caceres said.
Cira Quispe, a Nazca resident, said people flooded out of their homes, knelt in the streets and prayed for the persistent aftershocks to stop.

Most of the estimated population of 40,000 -- left without light, water or working telephones -- hauled their belongings into the streets and abandoned what was left of their houses in fear of another quake.
"We are going to have to sleep in the street," Quispe said as he waited for the army to fly in blankets and food.
Nazca is one of the main tourist attractions in Peru because of its mysterious pre-Inca lines that form patterns in the desert and can be seen only from the air.
The Andean country is prone to frequent seismic activity. On May 31, 1970, an earthquake measuring 7.8 in magnitude leveled scores of towns and caused slides of ice and mud that killed 67,000 people.
